title.value: Modeling Event Plausibility with Consistent Conceptual Abstraction
title.justification: Title is directly taken from the top of the document where the authors and their affiliations are mentioned.
title.quote:
Modeling Event Plausibility with Consistent Conceptual Abstraction

Ian Porada ^{1} , Kaheer Suleman ^{2} , Adam Trischler ^{2} , and Jackie Chi Kit Cheung ^{1}

analysis.description: The paper addresses the challenge of modeling event plausibility using Transformer-based models, specifically focusing on the inconsistency in conceptual abstraction within these models. It introduces methods to enforce consistency by leveraging lexical hierarchies, evaluating models' alignment with human judgments, and proposing improvements in plausibility prediction over lexical hierarchies.

type.justification: The paper involves experiments using Transformer models (like RoBERTa) and evaluates their performance on tasks that require human-like plausibility judgments, indicating empirical research.
type.quote: In this work, we show that Transformer-based plausibility models are markedly inconsistent across the conceptual classes of a lexical hierarchy, inferring that “a person breathing” is plausible while “a dentist breathing” is not, for example. We find this inconsistency persists even when models are softly injected with lexical knowledge, and we present a simple post-hoc method of forcing model consistency that improves correlation with human plausibility judgements.

name.justification: The paper is focused on semantic plausibility in natural language understanding, which is a key area of study within Natural Language Processing.
name.quote: Understanding natural language requires common sense, one aspect of which is the ability to discern the plausibility of events.

name.justification: The paper specifically deals with event plausibility which forms part of commonsense reasoning, exploring how models can align with human judgement in understanding commonsense knowledge.
name.quote: such as conditional commonsense inference (Gordon et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2017), abductive commonsense reasoning (Bhagavatula et al., 2020), and commonsense knowledge acquisition (Zhang et al., 2020a; Hwang et al., 2020).

name.justification: The work involves leveraging lexical hierarchies and analyzing semantic plausibility which falls under lexical semantics.
name.quote: we evaluate models by correlation with two datasets of human plausibility judgements. Our models build off of RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), a pre-trained Transformer masked language model. ^{1} We use WordNet 3.1 (Miller, 1995) hypernymy relations as a lexical hierarchy.
